subtopics.title: The Law of Universal Gravitation and Its Equation

questions.question: Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the force between two particles is:
options: Directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres
Directly proportional to the sum of the masses and inversely proportional to the distance
Inversely proportional to the product of the masses
Proportional to the distance between their surfaces

questions.question: The distance d in F = Gm₁m₂/d² is measured between the objects':
The gravitational force between two learners (50 kg and 70 kg) two metres apart is about 5,8 × 10⁻⁸ N. This shows that:
options: The law fails for small objects
The learners' masses were too small to attract at all
Gravity between everyday objects is far too weak to notice

questions.question: While the Earth pulls you down with 588 N, you pull the Earth:
options: Up with a much smaller force
Not at all — planets cannot be pulled
Up with a much larger force
Up with exactly 588 N — a Newton's third law pair

questions.question: Doubling the distance between two masses changes the gravitational force to:
options: One quarter of its original value

questions.question: Doubling BOTH masses (distance unchanged) multiplies the force by:
One mass is quadrupled and the distance is doubled. The new force is:
options: Exactly the original force — the factors cancel

questions.question: The force between two objects is 8 × 10⁻⁷ N. If the distance between their centres is halved, the new force is:

subtopics.title: Gravitational Acceleration from g Equals G M Over r Squared

questions.question: Setting mg equal to GMm/r² and cancelling m gives:
The cancellation of the small m means that:
options: Every object at the same place falls with the same acceleration
Gravity does not act on massive objects

questions.question: Using M = 4,87 × 10²⁴ kg and r = 6,05 × 10⁶ m, the surface gravity of Venus is about:
A satellite two Earth radii ABOVE the surface is three radii from the centre, so g there is:

subtopics.title: Weight on Other Planets and True Weightlessness

questions.question: Which pairing is correct?
options: Mass: kilograms, changes with location; weight: newtons, constant
Mass: newtons, constant; weight: kilograms, varies
Mass: kilograms, constant everywhere; weight: newtons, varies with g

questions.question: A 60 kg astronaut on the Moon (g = 1,62 m·s⁻²) weighs:
Astronauts aboard an orbiting station float because:
options: Gravity is zero at orbital height
Their mass becomes zero in orbit
The station's walls shield them from gravity
They and the station are in continuous free fall around the Earth, so no support force acts on them

questions.question: Weightlessness is best defined as:
options: Experiencing no support force while gravity still acts

questions.question: The word universal in the law's name means:
options: Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass
The law only applies beyond Earth
Only planets and stars attract things
Gravity is the strongest force in the universe

questions.question: You never feel your desk's gravitational pull because:
options: Desks are not massive enough to exert gravity at all
The desk's pull is cancelled by the Earth's
Gravity between everyday masses is far too weak to sense — a planet-sized partner is needed

questions.question: The Earth barely responds to your equal 588 N pull on it because:
options: Your pull is actually smaller than 588 N
The same force on an enormous mass produces an immeasurably small acceleration
The pull acts only on the Earth's surface

subtopics.title: Double the Distance, Quarter the Pull

questions.question: The torchlight picture works because gravity, like light, :
options: Spreads over four times the area at double the distance, so its strength quarters
Travels at the speed of sound
Gets absorbed by the air in between

questions.question: Tripling the distance between two objects divides the pull by:
Which change does NOT involve squaring?
When the distance doubles, the single most common error is to say the force:
options: Halves — forgetting that distance changes are squared

questions.question: A scale reading 60 on Earth reads about 10 on the Moon because:
options: The Moon pulls each kilogram with about a sixth of Earth's pull, and a scale is really a pull-meter
Two thirds of your mass stays on Earth
Scales are calibrated only for Earth rock

questions.question: Your mass on the Moon, compared with on Earth, is:
A planet's surface pull is decided by the fraction fight between:
options: Its day length and its orbit
Its mass on top and its radius squared underneath
Its density and its distance from the Sun

questions.question: The moment at the top of a trampoline bounce feels like astronaut weightlessness because:
options: Gravity switches off briefly at the top
Your mass decreases at the top of the bounce
The air supports you instead of the mat
Nothing is supporting you while gravity still acts — brief free fall
